newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO U.S. IN U.S. CENTS/LB, CIF.
Bull (95 Chemical Lean) 96 +3 on last week
Shank (90 CL) 88 +3
Trimmings (85 CL) 79 +0
Chucks (85 CL) 81 +3
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO JAPAN IN U.S. CENTS/LB CIF.
Chilled grassfed fullsets 131 n/con last week
Chilled grassfed loin:striploin 185 n/c
cube roll 240 +6
tender loin 440 n/c
Frozen Chuck/blade 93 +1
Frozen Thick flank 109 +4
Frozen Fore/hind blended 85 +3
Frozen Topside 114 +7
Frozen Silverside 103 +2
Frozen Brisket 82 +4

AMLC COMMENTARY: Despite scattered rainfall received in several regions during the past week (which did little more than settle the dust), the generally dry and cool seasonal conditions continued to characterise livestock markets.
Yardings are increasingly being dominated by lower finished stock, although good quality offerings are meeting firm demand.
Saleyards in both Queensland and New South Wales continue to feature large numbers of cows and heifers.
The proportion of female cattle entering the yards is reflected in the slaughter statistics - females comprised 45.5 percent of last week's throughput in Queensland.

Fortunately, a strengthening of the U.S. imported beef market in recent weeks has held cow prices firm in just about all Australian centres. This week, imported beef prices rose by an average 2 U.S. cents/lb. The improvement in prices was driven by firmer demand from U.S. traders covering short positions, combined with relatively tight supplies.
End user demand, however, remains subdued.
Since the beginning of June, 90CL manufacturing beef exports (when denominated in Australian currency) have gained 33c/kg, to reach their prestent level of 227c/kg.
A significant portion of this can be attributed to the depreciation in the Australian dollar.

The imported grinding beef market in the U.S. was firmer during this week's trading, supported by light offerings from overseas and stronger U.S. domestic prices for lean grinding meat. Most activity was by traders covering short positions, as end user demand was relatively quiet again this week.
Although participants reported the market as quiet on Thursday, the market remained steady throughout the week.
Spot meat continues to be available and is currently priced lower than the current CIF levels.
Little interest was evident for Australian round cuts this weak, as offerings from overseas were very tight.
Domestic grinding beef prices were mixed, rising by three USclb for lean beef, but falling three USc/lb for fattier grinding beef.
While wholesale beef prices in Japan remained stable this week, chilled grassfed fullsets traded six Ac/kg FAS lower, again due to the influence of exchange rates.
Barbecue items continue to be in demand by both Japanese restaurants and retailers.
For export steers conforming to Japanese market specifications, there was little variation on the price levels over the past couple of weeks. Most price quotes were plus or minus a few cents.
A noticable exception was for 100 day grainfed cattle which gained 10 c/kg in Queensland over the hooks trading.
The success achieved by Australian exporters in capturing the lion's hsare of last week's Korean tender, failed to produce a prounced effect on livestock markets this week.

However, the encouraging news is that 26,500 tonnes of beef remain to be purchased by Korean authorities between now and the end of September, indicating that at least two further tenders should be in the pipeline.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
